source: Woolley, Chabris, Pentland, Hashmi, Malone (2010) Evidence for a collective intelligence factor in the performance of human groups (Science 330)
finding: Founding idea. Collective intelligence c is defined as the general ability of a group to perform a wide variety of tasks. It is inferred when a group's score on one task correlates with its scores on other tasks. It is a property of the group, not only of its members.
numbers: Two studies, 699 people, 192 groups of 2 to 5 members (Study 1: 40 groups of 3; Study 2: 152 groups of 2 to 5).
quote: the general ability of the group to perform a wide variety of tasks
limits: Defined by analogy with Spearman g. The three tests of c (positive manifold, one dominant factor of 30-50%, not reducible to member IQ) follow Chabris 2007.
agent_relevance: Background only. Gives a vocabulary for cross-task generality of a scaffold.

source: Woolley, Chabris, Pentland, Hashmi, Malone (2010) Evidence for a collective intelligence factor in the performance of human groups (Science 330)
finding: Study 1 factor structure. Average inter-task correlation is positive. One factor dominates and a single-factor model fits.
numbers: Mean inter-item r = 0.28. First eigenvalue >43% of variance, second 18%. CFA: chi2 = 1.66, df = 5, p = 0.89, CFI = .99, RMSEA = 0.01. Tasks: brainstorming, matrix reasoning, moral reasoning, shopping trip planning, typing, plus a video game as criterion.
limits: Only 40 groups of strangers in one lab session. Tasks chosen by the authors from a group-task taxonomy.
agent_relevance: A 43% first factor is also what a few positively correlated tasks give.

source: Woolley, Chabris, Pentland, Hashmi, Malone (2010) Evidence for a collective intelligence factor in the performance of human groups (Science 330)
finding: Study 1 pairwise correlations (Table 1, n = 40 groups). The c score loads most on matrix reasoning and typing, least on brainstorming and moral reasoning.
numbers: r of group task with c: matrix reasoning 0.86, typing 0.80, shopping trip 0.66, video game 0.52, moral reasoning 0.42, brainstorming 0.38. Brainstorming correlates only 0.11 to 0.30 with other tasks. Avg member intelligence with c 0.19 (ns); max 0.27 (ns); avg and max member intelligence correlate 0.73 with each other.
limits: c score is built from the same tasks, so its correlation with each task is inflated (part-whole).
agent_relevance: Tasks with a single correct answer carry the factor; open-ended generation tasks carry little of it.

source: Woolley, Chabris, Pentland, Hashmi, Malone (2010) Evidence for a collective intelligence factor in the performance of human groups (Science 330)
finding: Study 2 replication in a larger sample with different group sizes and more tasks. First factor 44%, second 20%. A ten-task subset also gave one factor.
numbers: 152 groups of 2 to 5. CFA: chi2 = 5.85, df = 5, p = 0.32, CFI = .98, NFI = .89, RMSEA = 0.03. Parallel analysis keeps factors with eigenvalue above 1.38: one factor in each sample. Principal-axis extraction gives 31% (Study 1) and 35% (Study 2) for the ten-task analyses. Multi-group CFA: structures invariant (chi2 = 11.34, df = 14, p = 0.66). Comparison: Wonderlic items from 642 individuals, same scree shape.
limits: Replication by the same team with the same task family. The principal-axis share (31-35%) is lower than the 43-44% headline.
agent_relevance: Headline variance share depends on extraction method.

source: Woolley, Chabris, Pentland, Hashmi, Malone (2010) Evidence for a collective intelligence factor in the performance of human groups (Science 330)
finding: c predicts a held-out criterion task better than member intelligence. Study 1 criterion: video game. Study 2 criterion: architectural design task modelled on an R&D problem.
numbers: Study 1: c score with criterion r = 0.52, P = 0.01; avg member IQ r = 0.18 ns; max r = 0.13 ns. Regression: c b = 0.51 (P = 0.001); avg IQ b = 0.08 ns; max IQ b = 0.01 ns. Study 2: c b = 0.36 (P = 0.0001); avg IQ b = 0.05 ns; max IQ b = 0.12 ns (group size controlled). Same design task done alone by 63 individuals: IQ r = 0.33, P = 0.009.
limits: Only two criterion tasks. With n = 40 the r = 0.52 has a wide interval. Individual IQ was a short test (Wonderlic in Study 1).
agent_relevance: Evidence that general group performance is not the sum of member IQ, inside this paradigm.

source: Woolley, Chabris, Pentland, Hashmi, Malone (2010) Evidence for a collective intelligence factor in the performance of human groups (Science 330)
finding: c is only weakly related to member IQ when both studies are pooled.
numbers: Avg member IQ with c: r = 0.15, P = 0.04. Max member IQ with c: r = 0.19, P = 0.008.
limits: College samples give range restriction, which shrinks IQ correlations. Later studies dispute this.
agent_relevance: In agent groups the equivalent is base-model strength, which may matter far more.

source: Woolley, Chabris, Pentland, Hashmi, Malone (2010) Evidence for a collective intelligence factor in the performance of human groups (Science 330)
finding: What predicts c: social sensitivity, even turn-taking, share of women. Cohesion, motivation and satisfaction did not.
numbers: Avg social sensitivity (Reading the Mind in the Eyes): r = 0.26, P = 0.002. Variance in speaking turns (sociometric badges, subset): r = -0.41, P = 0.01. Proportion female: r = 0.23, P = 0.007, mediated by social sensitivity (Sobel z = 1.93, P = 0.03). Women scored higher on RME: t(441) = 3.42. In a joint regression only social sensitivity was significant (b = 0.33, P = 0.05).
quote: groups where a few people dominated the conversation were less collectively intelligent
limits: Correlational. Turn data exist only for a subset wearing badges. Gender share is confounded with sensitivity.
agent_relevance: Turn-taking skew is a measurable process signal. Loosely maps to one agent dominating a multi-agent thread.

source: Riedl, Kim, Gupta, Malone, Woolley (2021) Quantifying collective intelligence in human groups (PNAS)
finding: Largest test of c, by the original team. Pooled 22 studies. A single CI factor fits and a restricted factor predicts held-out tasks.
numbers: 22 studies, 1,356 groups, 5,279 individuals, groups of 2 to 7, 4 to 8 tasks per study, all run on the POGS online platform. Mean inter-task r = 0.27 (range 0.12 to 0.50). Loadings 0.27 to 0.52, average variance extracted 44%. Leave-one-task-out: mean r = 0.40 (95% CI 0.26 to 0.53), all P < 0.001.
quote: CI is most strongly predicted by group collaboration process, followed by individual skill and group composition
limits: All data come from one research network and one platform. Three tasks (brainstorm object, typing, unscramble words) appear in every study. Not an independent replication.
agent_relevance: Template for testing generality of a multi-part system: leave-one-task-out prediction.

source: Riedl, Kim, Gupta, Malone, Woolley (2021) Quantifying collective intelligence in human groups (PNAS)
finding: Process beats skill in the pooled data. Random forest on CI: collaboration process (skill congruence, strategy, effort) explained most, then individual skill (mean and max), then group size, social perceptiveness, composition. Skill congruence and strategy predict positively. Effort does not.
numbers: Proportion of women positive, mediated by social perceptiveness. Age diversity negative. Sudoku: over 51% of explained variation came from individual skill. Unscrambling words: 55% from process.
limits: Importance varies by task: puzzle tasks lean on skill, coordination tasks on process. Process measures come from platform logs.
agent_relevance: Contribution should match ability. In an agent group, route work to the strongest member.

source: Engel, Woolley, Jing, Chabris, Malone (2014) Reading the Mind in the Eyes or reading between the lines? Theory of mind predicts collective intelligence equally well online and face-to-face (PLoS ONE 9(12))
finding: Conceptual replication with a new task battery, face-to-face versus text-chat online. One factor in both. Reading the Mind in the Eyes predicts c equally well in both.
numbers: 68 groups randomly assigned: 32 face-to-face, 36 online. First factor 49% (face-to-face) and 41% (online); second factor less than half of that. RME with c: r = 0.52 (P = 0.002) face-to-face, r = 0.55 (P < .001) online. Percent female with c online: r = 0.41, P = 0.01. Mediation by RME: Sobel z = 1.95, P = 0.05.
quote: even though the online groups communicate only via text and never see each other at all
limits: Same lab team. Strangers. About one hour of tasks. n = 68.
agent_relevance: The social sensitivity effect survives a text-only channel. Relevant to text-only agent groups.

source: Engel, Woolley, Jing, Chabris, Malone (2014) Reading the Mind in the Eyes or reading between the lines? Theory of mind predicts collective intelligence equally well online and face-to-face (PLoS ONE 9(12))
finding: Communication process in both modes. More total communication goes with higher c. Unequal participation and unequal work contribution go with lower c.
numbers: Distribution of communication (SD across members) negatively correlated with c in both modes (face-to-face r about -0.41 in the table as parsed; table layout in the PDF text was jumbled, so treat exact cells as approximate). Regressions with RME plus amount and distribution of communication: both matter about equally in the two conditions.
quote: groups in which one or two people dominated the discussion and activity were less collectively intelligent
limits: Exact table cells not reliably extracted. Text statements are reliable, individual cell numbers are not.
agent_relevance: Dominance by one voice hurts; supports the guardrail against one agent steering all others.

source: Rowe, Hattie, Hester (2021) g versus c: comparing individual and collective intelligence across two meta-analyses (Cognitive Research 6:26)
finding: Independent meta-analysis. 14 studies, 19 samples, 1,359 groups of 2 to 6. Mean first-factor variance 43% (SD 3.6%). c to criterion tasks: random-effects r = 0.26 (95% CI .10 to .40), high heterogeneity.
numbers: c with criterion: 9 effects from 8 samples, N = 857 groups. Q(8) = 59.36, p < .001, I2 = 86.5%, tau2 = .05. Average member IQ with criterion (6 samples, N = 366 groups): r = .06 (95% CI -.08 to .20), I2 = 35%. Average variance extracted by c over 49 loadings: 30.23% (22% to 37%), below the 50% rule. About 80% of studies lacked power. Only 6 of 19 samples had enough groups for r = .10 to .30 (84 to 782 groups needed).
limits: Only 7 of 19 samples were independent of Woolley and co-authors. Authors advise not adopting c until more evidence accumulates.
agent_relevance: The effect is moderate and uncertain. Do not treat a group factor as settled.

source: Rowe, Hattie, Hester (2021) g versus c: comparing individual and collective intelligence across two meta-analyses (Cognitive Research 6:26)
finding: Failed-replication pattern reported in the review. Woolley-affiliated attempts all reproduced c. Independent attempts all partly or wholly failed. Barlow and Dennis (2016) rejected c with 3 tasks. Bates and Gupta (2017) found member IQ explains most of group IQ.
numbers: Barlow tasks (brainstorm, college admissions, shopping trip): the criterion candy-factory task correlated .02, .01, .15 with them. Bates and Gupta: group IQ and average member IQ covaried 'indistinguishable from 100%' (as cited), average member IQ accounting for over 80% of variance in group scores; first factor about 50% in their study 2. Credé and Howardson (2017) reanalysed 6 samples (N = 487 groups) and concluded the data do not support a general factor explaining substantial variance across a wide range of group tasks.
limits: SECOND-HAND. The original Bates and Gupta and Credé and Howardson papers were not opened (publisher pages gave 403 or empty). Three-task batteries can fail for psychometric reasons.
agent_relevance: Competing account: group factor equals aggregated member g. For agents, a stronger base model may explain most group score.

source: Rowe, Hattie, Hester (2021) g versus c: comparing individual and collective intelligence across two meta-analyses (Cognitive Research 6:26)
finding: Methodological critique of the group-IQ paradigm: tasks chosen by face validity, few and short, low reliability, subtest order rarely randomised, little control of individual g, weak criterion tasks.
numbers: Average battery 6.3 subtests. 14 of 19 samples in a lab. 11 of 18 samples in the USA. Imbimbo et al. (2020), cited: 550 high-school students, 110 groups of 5, Raven's APM odd and even halves; majority-vote success at group level follows individual success probability strongly.
limits: Imbimbo is second-hand. Group tasks and individual IQ are rarely measured on matched items.
agent_relevance: A c built on few unreliable tasks is weak evidence. Build any agent benchmark with many reliable items.

source: A recipe for dyadic collective intelligence for well-structured tasks: mix equal parts cognitive ability and confidence (2025, Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications; author list not recorded)
finding: Independent re-test in dyads with well-structured tasks aligned to the Cattell-Horn-Carroll model. Individual intelligence and confidence were the strongest predictors of dyadic CI. Turn-taking equality and gender composition did not replicate. Social sensitivity did.
numbers: 105 undergraduate dyads, 3 tasks kept after dropping an unreliable geography test (loading 0.21). Hierarchical regression on CI, final block: individual intelligence (Raven) beta = 0.33 (p < .01); confidence beta = 0.32 (p < .001); social sensitivity beta = 0.22 (p < .01); turn-taking inequality beta = 0.08 (p = .24, ns); all-female dyads beta = -0.54 (p = .01). Block 3 added delta R2 = 0.25. Final R2 = 0.60. Individual intelligence with CI r = 0.65. CI and collective confidence factors r = 0.85 but a one-factor model fit poorly (RMSEA 0.25).
quote: Individual intelligence and confidence were the strongest predictors of dyadic CI for well-structured tasks
limits: Dyads only, undergraduates, three tasks. Task type is the boundary: well-structured single-answer tasks.
agent_relevance: For closed benchmark tasks the group score tracks member ability and confidence. Agent groups mostly meet such tasks.

source: Ilic and Gignac (2024) Evidence of interrelated cognitive-like capabilities in large language models: indications of artificial general intelligence or achievement? (Intelligence 106)
finding: Single LLMs show a strong positive manifold and a general factor. Not a group study but the baseline for any LLM c claim.
numbers: 591 LLMs, 12 benchmarks. Mean inter-test r = 0.73 (0.63 for the six short tests) against 0.45 to 0.50 in humans. General factor about 66% of variance (65.6%) against 40 to 50% in humans. Omega hierarchical 0.94. Parameter count with the factor r = 0.54 (95% CI .48 to .59), diminishing returns.
limits: Models share training data and many are fine-tunes of each other, so rows are not independent. Benchmark contamination possible.
agent_relevance: A bigger first factor is normal for LLMs, so a 66% group factor is weak evidence of anything group-specific.

source: Zhou, Liu, Liu, Wang, Shao, Xu, Jin, Li (2026) Identifying collective intelligence factor in LLM agent groups for generalizable multi-agent system design (Findings of ACL 2026)
finding: First direct LLM analogue of Woolley. 108 LLM agent groups from 8 LLMs, sizes 3/5/8, 2 or 3 rounds, 3 topologies, homogeneous or mixed models, run on 5 tasks. One Artificial CI (ACI) factor explains 66.3%.
numbers: Tasks: commonsense, math, games, coding, writing. Mean inter-task r = 0.55. EFA: first factor 66.3%, second 18.7%. CFA single factor: chi2 = 30.6, p < 0.001, CFI = 0.967. Models: gpt-3.5-turbo, gpt-4o-mini, Qwen2.5-7B/32B/72B, glm-4-9b, internlm2.5-20b, gemma-2-27b. Single-model task averages 0.40 to 0.81. ACI scaled to mean 100, SD 15.
limits: Only 5 tasks and 108 groups. Groups share base models so rows are not independent. The paper compares its 0.55 with 0.28 and attributes 0.28 to Riedl 2021; 0.28 is from Woolley 2010 (Riedl reports 0.27). The CFA chi2 p < 0.001 rejects exact fit.
agent_relevance: Cross-task generality exists across agent-group configurations, plausibly because stronger models and better wiring help everywhere.

source: Zhou, Liu, Liu, Wang, Shao, Xu, Jin, Li (2026) Identifying collective intelligence factor in LLM agent groups for generalizable multi-agent system design (Findings of ACL 2026)
finding: Leave-one-task-out and drivers of ACI. Collaboration process predicts ACI more than individual intelligence. Group size matters little.
numbers: Leave-one-out ACI correlation with held-out task above 0.8 on three tasks and about 0.5 on the others, all p < 0.001. Random forest: skill congruence (correlation of agent ability with node degree) over 50% of importance, average individual g 37%, max g, group size and effort each under 5%. Case: group with Qwen2.5-72B (g = 119.9) had ACI 98.8 and 75% higher cost; group with internlm2.5-20b (g = 92.1) had 9.7% higher ACI.
quote: skill congruence and average individual intelligence are both significant positive predictors of ACI
limits: Process variables are the authors' own proxies (variance of node degree stands in for turn-taking inequality). The 'process' is graph structure, not free conversation. One paper, no independent replication known to this note.
agent_relevance: Put the strongest model at the hub; ability should match connection. Fits the guardrail that structure beats headcount.

source: Zhou, Liu, Liu, Wang, Shao, Xu, Jin, Li (2026) Identifying collective intelligence factor in LLM agent groups for generalizable multi-agent system design (Findings of ACL 2026)
finding: Centralised versus decentralised networks, and ACI as a design tool. Strongest LLM as central node gave best centralised groups and could beat the decentralised group at lower cost. Predicted ACI used as a regulariser for GPTSwarm and G-Designer raised unseen-task accuracy.
numbers: 2-fold cross-validation: R2 above 0.8 for ACI, above 0.6 on most tasks. Predicted-ACI leave-one-task-out r above 0.6 on commonsense, math and coding, beating a simple average baseline. GPTSwarm: commonsense 0.75 to 0.77, math 0.81 to 0.91, game 0.50 to 0.53, coding 0.87 to 0.89, writing 0.88 to 0.89 (gains 1.1% to 12.3%). G-Designer gains 2.3% to 7.8%. Authors report an average gain of 4.6% on unseen tasks.
limits: Gains are small outside math. Number of seeds not seen in the text read. The G-Designer table rows were garbled in the PDF text, so only the stated range is recorded.
agent_relevance: A 4.6% gain from a regulariser is a small lever.

source: Riedl (2026) Emergent coordination in multi-agent language models (ICLR 2026; arXiv 2510.05174)
finding: Information-theoretic test of whether an LLM group is more than a set of agents, using a group guessing game with no direct communication. A theory-of-mind prompt moved groups from chaotic to coordinated.
numbers: GPT-4.1, 7,150 preliminary runs (13 group sizes from 3 to 15 x 11 temperatures x 50). Each extra member cut odds of success about 8% (OR 0.92, p < 1e-16). Each +1 temperature raised odds about 50% (OR 1.50). Main: N = 10, T = 1, 200 runs per condition (plain, persona, persona plus 'think about what others might do'), 600 total. Success rates not significantly different. Triadic information I3 about 0 in plain (p = 0.974) and persona (p = 0.846) but positive in the ToM condition (p = 3.5e-14). Same pattern across Llama-3.1-8B and 70B, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Qwen3-235B.
limits: The ToM prompt gave no gain in success rate. The measure describes statistical structure, not accuracy. One game.
agent_relevance: Prompting for theory of mind changes how agents align, echoing the human theory-of-mind link to c, but no accuracy benefit is shown.

source: Fan et al. (2026) Towards a science of collective AI: LLM-based multi-agent systems need a transition from blind trial-and-error to rigorous science (arXiv 2602.05289)
finding: Position paper. Argues that multi-agent claims need a collaboration gain metric that compares the system with a single agent at equal compute, so extra tokens are not read as collective intelligence. It does not test a c factor.
numbers: Gain metric: Gamma above 1 means genuine collaboration gain, below 1 means resource redundancy. One topology pre-experiment and one case study. Cites Woolley 2010 only in passing.
limits: Position paper with small illustrative experiments. I read the front matter, definition and appendix headings, not all figures.
agent_relevance: Strong fit with our guardrails: always compare against one agent with equal compute before claiming a group effect.

source: Huang, Zhao, Yi, Xie (2025) On the dynamics of multi-agent LLM communities driven by value diversity (arXiv 2512.10665)
finding: Calls collective intelligence the 'c-factor' in the introduction but measures emergent social behaviour, not cross-task ability. LLaMA-3.1-70B agents with value personas, groups of 4, 10, 30. Value diversity raises stability and creativity of constitutions, with diminishing returns, and extreme heterogeneity causes instability.
numbers: Group sizes 4, 10, 30. From 4 to 10 agents gave a large jump in emergent behaviour, 10 to 30 a smaller one. Stage 1: 25 chat rounds, then constitution writing. One condition kept Rousseauian principles 80.3% while Lockean rules rose to 15.7% (conditions not recorded).
limits: Not a c-factor test. No task battery. Outcome coding is simulation-specific.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence. Value diversity may help open-ended tasks but is not shown to help closed-task accuracy.

source: Collective intelligence in teams: contextualizing collective intelligent behavior over time (2022, Frontiers in Psychology; author list not recorded)
finding: Conceptual critique. Team CI should be defined by interaction processes that fit task demands over time, not by outcome scores alone. Calls for fine-grained longitudinal process data.
numbers: No new data in the part read (abstract and introduction only).
quote: Teams behave collectively intelligent when the collective behaviors during the collaboration period are in line with the requirements
limits: Only abstract and introduction read.
agent_relevance: Supports logging who contributes what and when rather than one final score.

source: Rowe, Hattie, Hester (2021) g versus c: comparing individual and collective intelligence across two meta-analyses (Cognitive Research 6:26)
finding: Three criteria for calling a factor c, taken from Woolley 2010 and Chabris 2007, and how the field has used them. The paradigm: 2 to 6 members, 5 to 10 tasks (matrix reasoning, shopping plan, brainstorming, word unscrambling), up to 1 to 2 hours, free discussion.
numbers: Criteria: (1) one factor explaining 30 to 50% of variance; (2) first factor at least double the second; (3) not explained by average member intelligence. Earlier meta-analyses of member IQ and group performance (Devine and Philips 2001, Stewart 2006, Bell 2007): pooled r = .28 (95% CI .25 to .30).
limits: Second-hand summary of the criteria. The ratio 'first at least double second' is met in Woolley (43 vs 18, 44 vs 20).
agent_relevance: Gives a checklist for judging any claimed LLM-group c.

source: Rowe, Hattie, Hester (2021) g versus c: comparing individual and collective intelligence across two meta-analyses (Cognitive Research 6:26)
finding: Claimed external links of c (all by the Woolley network, as listed by Rowe): business performance, team learning, academic achievement, scientific teams, competitive video-game teams, high-stakes decisions, and cross-cultural replication.
numbers: Rowe lists Engel et al. 2015 (cultures), Mayo and Woolley 2017 (business), Kim et al. 2017 (video-game teams), Radcliffe et al. 2019 and Rogers et al. 2019 (high-stakes decisions). Rowe pooled correlations of c with such criteria r = .26.
limits: Titles only; these primary papers were not opened by this agent.
agent_relevance: Real-world validity is claimed but sparse and mostly within one network.
